questions.stem: Why must the amount of DNA in a cell double before it divides?
options: So that each daughter cell receives a complete copy of the genetic material
So that each daughter cell receives twice as much DNA as the parent cell had
So that the cell can make enough ribosomes for the division itself
So that half of the DNA can be broken down to supply energy during the division
questions.explanation: DNA replication before division produces two identical copies of every chromosome, so each daughter cell gets a full set of genetic information. Daughter cells from mitosis have the same amount of DNA as the parent cell had before replication.

questions.stem: A cell in G1 contains 6 picograms of DNA. How much DNA will it contain at the end of S phase, and how much will each daughter cell contain after mitosis?
options: 12 pg, then 6 pg in each daughter cell
12 pg, then 12 pg in each daughter cell
6 pg, then 3 pg in each daughter cell
3 pg, then 6 pg in each daughter cell
questions.explanation: DNA replicates during S phase, doubling the amount to 12 pg. Mitosis then shares the copies equally, so each daughter cell returns to 6 pg, the same as the original cell in G1.

questions.stem: Which process do prokaryotic cells use to divide?
options: Meiosis
Fertilisation
Binary fission
Mitosis
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes divide by binary fission: the circular chromosome is replicated, the two copies separate as the cell elongates, and the cell divides in two. Mitosis and meiosis are divisions of eukaryotic nuclei.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the products of binary fission and mitosis?
options: Binary fission gives four haploid cells, while mitosis gives two diploid cells
Binary fission gives genetically varied cells; mitosis gives identical ones
Mitosis halves the chromosome number; binary fission keeps it the same
Both give two cells with the same number and type of chromosomes as the parent
questions.explanation: The products of both binary fission and mitosis are genetically identical to the parent, with the same number and type of chromosomes, barring mutation. Halving and variation are features of meiosis.

questions.stem: In which phase of mitosis do chromosomes condense and become visible, and the nuclear membrane break down?
options: Anaphase
Telophase
Prophase
Metaphase
questions.explanation: In prophase, chromosomes coil up and become visible as two sister chromatids, the spindle begins to form and the nuclear membrane breaks down. Chromosomes line up in metaphase and separate in anaphase.

questions.stem: In which phase of mitosis do nuclear membranes re-form around two sets of chromosomes at opposite ends of the cell?
options: Metaphase
Telophase
Anaphase
Prophase
questions.explanation: In telophase, the separated chromosomes reach the poles, uncoil, and new nuclear membranes form around each set. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm into two cells.

questions.stem: In an onion root tip, 200 cells are counted: 170 in interphase, 14 in prophase, 6 in metaphase, 4 in anaphase and 6 in telophase. What can be concluded?
options: Cells spend most of the cell cycle in interphase, and prophase is the longest phase of mitosis
Cells spend most of the cell cycle in mitosis, and anaphase is the longest phase of mitosis
Interphase is shorter than any phase of mitosis, because interphase is not a stage of cell division
All phases of mitosis take exactly the same time, because they are equally likely to be seen
questions.explanation: The proportion of cells in each stage reflects the relative time spent there. With 85% of cells in interphase and more in prophase (14) than in any other phase of mitosis, interphase is longest overall and prophase is the longest phase of mitosis.

questions.stem: What are homologous chromosomes?
options: A pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, carrying the same genes
Two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere after replication
Two chromosomes from the same parent that carry different genes
The sex chromosomes X and Y, which are always identical in males
questions.explanation: Diploid cells contain pairs of homologous chromosomes, one inherited from each parent, carrying the same genes at the same positions, though possibly different alleles. Sister chromatids are the two identical copies made by replication.

questions.stem: A species has a diploid number of 2n = 18. How many chromosomes are in each of its gametes?
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, producing haploid gametes with one chromosome from each homologous pair: 18 / 2 = 9. Fertilisation then restores the diploid number of 18.

questions.stem: Why are the products of meiosis haploid?
options: Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis I, so each cell keeps one of each pair
Sister chromatids separate in meiosis I, so each cell keeps half of each chromosome
The DNA is not replicated before meiosis, so half of it is missing
Half of the chromosomes are broken down by lysosomes during meiosis II
questions.explanation: In meiosis I, the members of each homologous pair move to opposite poles, so each daughter cell receives one chromosome from each pair: a single set. Meiosis II then separates sister chromatids, as in mitosis.

questions.stem: In which phase of meiosis do homologous chromosome pairs line up together across the equator of the cell?
options: Metaphase II
Anaphase II
Telophase II
Metaphase I
questions.explanation: In metaphase I, homologous chromosomes line up in pairs at the equator. In metaphase II, single chromosomes (each still made of two chromatids) line up, as in mitosis.

questions.stem: A cell is seen dividing with sister chromatids separating to opposite poles. The cell has 4 chromatids moving to each pole, and the organism's diploid number is 8. Which division is this?
options: Anaphase II of meiosis
Anaphase of mitosis
Anaphase I of meiosis
Metaphase I of meiosis
questions.explanation: Sister chromatids separate in mitotic anaphase and in anaphase II. In mitosis each pole would receive 8 chromatids (one per chromosome of the diploid set), but here each receives 4, the haploid number, so the cell is in anaphase II. In anaphase I, whole homologues, not chromatids, separate.

questions.stem: When does crossing over occur?
options: In anaphase of mitosis, between sister chromatids
In telophase II of meiosis, between daughter nuclei
In interphase, between the two strands of one DNA molecule
In prophase I of meiosis, between homologous chromosomes
questions.explanation: During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange segments of chromatids at crossover points. This produces chromatids with new combinations of alleles.

questions.stem: Why is crossing over important?
options: It creates new combinations of alleles on each chromosome
It doubles the number of chromosomes passed to each gamete
It makes sure all gametes carry identical sets of alleles
It repairs any mutations present in the parent's chromosomes
questions.explanation: Crossing over exchanges segments between homologous chromosomes, recombining alleles so that chromatids carry combinations not found in either parent. This increases genetic variation among gametes.

questions.stem: An organism has a diploid number of 2n = 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can it produce by independent assortment?
questions.explanation: With n = 4 homologous pairs, each pair can line up in two orientations at metaphase I, giving 2 to the power of 4 = 16 combinations. Using 2 to the power of 8 confuses the diploid number with the number of pairs.

questions.stem: Which statement describes independent assortment in meiosis?
options: The random orientation of each homologous pair at metaphase I
The exchange of segments between chromatids of a homologous pair
The random fusion of one egg with one of many sperm cells
The copying of each chromosome to form two sister chromatids
questions.explanation: Each homologous pair lines up independently of the others at metaphase I, so the maternal and paternal chromosomes are shuffled into many combinations in the gametes. Exchange of segments is crossing over.

questions.stem: What is the effect of fertilisation on chromosome number?
options: It doubles the diploid number to make a tetraploid zygote
It restores the diploid number by combining two haploid gametes
It halves the chromosome number by removing one set from the zygote
It keeps the haploid number by joining two haploid nuclei side by side
questions.explanation: A haploid sperm (n) fuses with a haploid egg (n) to give a diploid zygote (2n). Meiosis and fertilisation together keep the chromosome number constant from generation to generation.

questions.stem: Which comparison of the products of mitosis and meiosis is correct?
options: Mitosis: two identical diploid cells; meiosis: four genetically different haploid cells
Mitosis: four different haploid cells; meiosis: two identical diploid cells
Mitosis: two different haploid cells; meiosis: four identical diploid cells
Both give two identical cells, but meiosis happens only in the gonads of adult animals
questions.explanation: Mitosis of a diploid cell produces two genetically identical diploid cells for growth and repair. Meiosis produces four haploid cells that differ genetically because of crossing over and independent assortment.

questions.stem: A strawberry plant reproduces by runners (asexually) and also by seeds (sexually). Which statement about the variation in its offspring is correct?
options: Both types of offspring vary equally, because they share the same parent plant
Runner plants vary only through new mutations; seedlings also vary by meiosis and fertilisation
Runner plants vary more than the seedlings do, because mitosis thoroughly mixes up the parent's alleles
Seedlings are identical to the parent, because seeds are formed by mitosis only
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction uses mitosis, so offspring are clones and differ only through mutation. Sexual reproduction adds variation from crossing over, independent assortment and the random combination of gametes at fertilisation.

questions.stem: During which stage of the cell cycle is DNA replicated?
options: S phase of interphase
G1 phase of interphase
Prophase of mitosis
Cytokinesis
questions.explanation: Interphase consists of G1 (growth), S (synthesis of DNA by replication) and G2 (further growth and preparation). Mitosis and cytokinesis follow.

questions.stem: What is the role of checkpoints in the cell cycle?
options: They mark where the cell will split in two during cytokinesis
They check conditions such as DNA damage before the cycle continues
They speed up DNA replication so that the next division can begin much sooner
They allow cells to divide without making new copies of their DNA
questions.explanation: Checkpoints are control points, such as at the end of G1, the end of G2 and during mitosis, where proteins check whether the cell is large enough, the DNA is undamaged and fully replicated, and chromosomes are attached to the spindle.

questions.stem: At one checkpoint, division halts until every chromosome is attached to spindle fibres. Which problem is this checkpoint mainly preventing?
options: Daughter cells receiving the wrong number of chromosomes
Daughter cells receiving unreplicated, single-stranded DNA
Daughter cells being too small to take in nutrients
Daughter cells receiving too few mitochondria from the parent
questions.explanation: The checkpoint during mitosis stops anaphase until all chromosomes are attached to the spindle. If chromatids separated without proper attachment, daughter cells could gain or lose chromosomes.

questions.stem: How do genes control the cell cycle?
options: They make glucose, which provides the signal for cells to divide
They code for proteins that promote or stop progress through the cycle
They change their own DNA sequence at each checkpoint so as to allow division
They leave the nucleus during interphase and divide the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Cells produce gene products, mostly proteins, that regulate the cell cycle. Some drive the cell forward to the next stage, and others halt it, for example when DNA is damaged.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a hormone that regulates cell division?
options: Adrenaline, which stops cells dividing permanently after the age of 18
Thyroxine, which causes every cell to divide by meiosis instead of mitosis
Human growth hormone, which stimulates cell division in growing tissues
Insulin, which halts all cell division whenever blood glucose is high
questions.explanation: Human growth hormone, released by the pituitary gland, stimulates cell division and growth in tissues such as bone and muscle. Hormones can therefore act as external signals that regulate the cell cycle.

questions.stem: How do carcinogens such as components of tobacco smoke lead to cancer?
options: They cause mutations in genes that regulate cell division
They speed up the S phase so cells copy DNA too accurately
They supply extra glucose so that every cell divides more
They stop cells from carrying out any mitosis or cytokinesis
questions.explanation: Carcinogens damage DNA, causing mutations in key regulatory genes. If genes that normally stop division are disabled or genes that drive division become overactive, cells divide uncontrollably and can form a tumour.

questions.stem: Why does cancer usually take many years to develop after exposure to a carcinogen such as asbestos?
options: Asbestos must be fully digested by lysosomes before any effect on cells occurs
Cancer cells divide much more slowly than normal cells at first
Only gametes are affected, so cancer appears in the next generation
Several mutations in different regulatory genes usually build up first
questions.explanation: Most cancers need mutations in several genes that control the cell cycle, which accumulate over time. This is why risk increases with longer exposure and with age.

questions.stem: Which is a carcinogen?
options: Asbestos fibres
Vitamin C
Dietary fibre
Distilled water
questions.explanation: Asbestos is a known carcinogen, linked to lung cancer and mesothelioma. Other examples include components of tobacco smoke and some dioxins.

questions.stem: Which conditions are needed to culture human cells in the laboratory?
options: Pure water, high salt and a temperature of about 60 °C
Sterile technique, nutrient medium, about 37 °C and controlled pH
Bright light, carbon dioxide only and a temperature close to 0 °C
Dry air, no nutrients and contact with soil bacteria for growth
questions.explanation: Cultured cells need a sterile environment, a medium supplying nutrients such as glucose, amino acids and growth factors, a suitable temperature (about 37 °C for human cells), controlled pH and regular removal of wastes.

questions.stem: Why must cell culture medium be replaced regularly?
options: To supply fresh nutrients and remove wastes that would harm the cells
To stop the cells from dividing by removing all of their growth factors from the flask
To add bacteria that help the human cells to grow and divide
To lower the temperature so the cells divide more quickly
questions.explanation: As cells grow they use up nutrients and release wastes such as lactic acid, which change the pH and can become toxic. Replacing the medium maintains suitable conditions.

questions.stem: Why is aseptic (sterile) technique essential in cell culture?
options: Sterile technique makes the cultured cells divide by meiosis
Sterile technique removes the need for any nutrient medium
Bacteria and fungi grow faster than animal cells and would take over
Microbes are needed to provide nutrients, so they must be counted and added to the culture
questions.explanation: Contaminating microorganisms multiply much faster than animal cells, using up nutrients and producing toxins, so they would ruin the culture. Sterile equipment and technique prevent contamination.

questions.stem: HeLa cells, cultured from a patient's cervical cancer in 1951, are still dividing in laboratories. Why are they especially useful, and what ethical issue do they raise?
options: They stop dividing after a few weeks, and were taken with full informed consent
They are haploid cells, and their use is limited by a ban on all cell culture
They divide only by meiosis, and they are owned by the patient's descendants
They divide indefinitely, but were taken without the patient's informed consent
questions.explanation: Unlike most normal cells, which stop dividing after a limited number of divisions, HeLa cells keep dividing, making them valuable for research such as vaccine development. They were taken without the patient's knowledge or consent, raising issues of consent and privacy.

questions.stem: Which is an application of cell culture?
options: Growing sheets of a patient's own skin cells to treat severe burns
Producing brand new species by fusing the cultured cells of two different animals
Making cells resistant to all diseases by culturing them in sugar
Replacing meiosis in humans so that all children are clones
questions.explanation: Skin cells taken from a burns patient can be cultured to produce more cells for grafts, reducing rejection because they are the patient's own. Cell cultures are also used to produce vaccines and to test drugs.

questions.stem: How does plant tissue culture produce many new plants from one parent?
options: Pollen is fused in culture to produce haploid adult plants
Leaves are ground up so that each cell becomes a new species
Small pieces of tissue grow on sterile medium with hormones into clones
Seeds are germinated in a sterile medium to produce many genetically varied offspring
questions.explanation: In micropropagation, small pieces of plant tissue are grown on a sterile medium containing nutrients and plant hormones, forming new plants by mitosis. The plants are genetically identical clones of the parent.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of using cultured cells to test a new drug?
options: Cultured cells cannot take in any substance at all from their liquid growth medium
Cultured cells are always bacteria, so results never apply to humans
Cells in a dish may respond differently from cells within the whole body
Cultured cells contain no DNA, so drugs cannot affect their metabolism
questions.explanation: Cultured cells lack the surrounding tissues, blood supply, hormones and immune responses of a living body, so a drug's effects in culture may not match its effects in a patient. Further testing is needed.

questions.stem: A culture of normal human skin cells stops dividing after about 50 divisions, but a culture of tumour cells keeps dividing. What does this suggest about the tumour cells?
options: The normal cells were contaminated, so they could not divide again
Mutations have disabled the normal controls that limit cell division
The tumour cells have lost all of their chromosomes during the many weeks in culture
The tumour cells divide by binary fission rather than by mitosis
questions.explanation: Normal cells have a limited number of divisions controlled by their genes. Tumour cells often carry mutations that remove these limits and bypass checkpoints, letting them divide indefinitely.

questions.stem: Which type of cell division produces gametes from germ-line cells in animals?
options: Cytokinesis only
Meiosis
Mitosis
Binary fission
questions.explanation: Germ-line cells in the ovaries and testes divide by meiosis to produce haploid gametes. Somatic (body) cells divide by mitosis for growth and repair.
